694.title: Magha Puja, deeper
694.hook: the verses taught that day: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind (Dhammapada 183–185)
694.howItsDone: On Magha Puja, Theravada Buddhists in Thailand, Laos and Cambodia visit temples, keep precepts, listen to teachings and walk three times around a shrine at dusk carrying candles, incense and flowers; the Ovada Patimokkha verses are often chanted.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Losar, the Tibetan new year, and your line, a fresh year. Did you clean your corner, and let something old be over? Today, a full moon in Thailand. Day six hundred ninety-four.

If someone stopped you on the street and said: the whole Buddhist path, in one breath, go. What would you say? The commentaries tell of a night when the Buddha did exactly that. On the full moon of the third lunar month, they say, twelve hundred and fifty monks came to the Bamboo Grove near Rajagaha, without being called. And he gave them the whole teaching in three short verses. In Thailand, Laos and Cambodia, that night is Magha Puja. Today we go deeper, into the verses themselves.
screen: `THE WHOLE PATH IN ONE BREATH.` → `1,250 MONKS, UNCALLED.` → `THREE SHORT VERSES.`

segments.voice: The verses are known as the Ovada Patimokkha, the exhortation. They're also in the Dhammapada, numbers 183 to 185. Here's the first, in Max Müller's translation: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." Three moves. First, stop. Don't do harm. That comes first because it's the floor: you can't build anything on a life that's hurting people. Second, do good. Not just avoid the bad, but actually reach for the skillful: kindness, giving, honesty. Third, purify the mind. Clear the inner water so you can see. That's meditation and wisdom. Notice something. The first two are the kind of advice any grandparent might give. Only the third is unusual. And yet the verse says all the Awakened teach all three, as one. The second verse, paraphrased, says patience is the highest austerity, and nirvana the highest thing of all. Someone who harms others isn't a true renunciant, however they dress. The third verse is almost a checklist: don't insult, don't harm, keep the training, be moderate in food, find a quiet place to sit, and work at the higher mind. There's an old story people tell about this. A poet asks a Chinese Chan master, Niaoke, for the essence of Buddhism. The master gives him this first verse. The poet scoffs: a three-year-old knows that. The master answers: a three-year-old may know it, but an eighty-year-old still can't do it. That's the heart of it. The teaching isn't hidden. It's hard because it's simple.
screen: `THE TEACHING IN THREE MOVES.` · `STOP, DO GOOD, CLEAR THE MIND.` · `PATIENCE AND A QUIET SEAT.` · `A CHILD KNOWS IT, AN ELDER TRIES.` · then, large: `THE HEART OF IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do all three today. Start now, sitting. That's the third one: clear the mind. Just follow the breath in and out, and let the water settle. Then, before the bell, choose the other two. One harm you'll hold back from today: a sharp word, a careless habit. And one good thing you'll actually do: a call, a gift, a hand. Hold both in mind, simply, and come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Magha Puja. The full-moon day remembering the gathering of the twelve hundred and fifty, and the verses: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind. Today's word.
Your line: the heart of it. Tonight, before sleep, check all three: what harm did you skip, what good did you do, and when did your mind clear? Day six hundred ninety-four.

pairs: monks who came without being called

myth: the verses taught that night are also in the Dhammapada
they are Dhammapada 183 to 185, the Ovada Patimokkha.
the first verse is a secret teaching for advanced monks
it's plain enough for a child; the story says the hard part is doing it.
the second verse calls patience the highest austerity
and nirvana the highest thing; someone who harms others isn't a true renunciant.

fork.setup: a poet asks a master for the essence of Buddhism. he hears: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind. 'a child knows that,' he says. what does the master answer?
options: 'then you're ready for the secret teaching.'
'a child may know it, but an old man still can't do it.'
fork.reveal: in the story people tell of Niaoke and the poet Bai Juyi, the point is that knowing is easy and doing is the life's work.

original.note: Pali, the opening of Dhammapada 183: the not-doing of all evil.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism is mostly meditation.
what it means: the summary verse puts not harming and doing good first, then clearing the mind.
what a scholar hears: Ovada Patimokkha, the exhortation, distinct from the longer monastic rule recited each fortnight.

sources.ref: Dhammapada commentary / Mahapadana Sutta (DN 14) tradition of the Ovada Patimokkha; the gathering of 1,250 at Veluvana

695.title: Saga Dawa
695.hook: the Tibetan month of the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing, when good deeds are said to multiply
695.tomorrow: Year two close: his own words
695.howItsDone: During Saga Dawa many Tibetan Buddhists walk pilgrim circuits such as the Lingkhor around Lhasa, give to beggars and monasteries, free animals, keep vegetarian, recite mantras and make offerings, especially on the full moon of Saga Dawa Duchen.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Magha Puja, and three short verses, and your line, the heart of it. Did you check all three last night: a harm skipped, a good done, a moment of clear mind? Day six hundred ninety-five.

Picture Lhasa early on a spring morning. Thousands of people are walking the same circle around the old city, clockwise, spinning prayer wheels, murmuring mantras. Some stop at every few steps to bow all the way to the ground. Along the route, beggars sit with open bowls, and people press small notes into every one. It's not a single holy day. It's a whole month. In Tibet, this is Saga Dawa.
screen: `A CIRCLE AROUND LHASA.` → `BOWLS ALONG THE ROUTE.` → `A WHOLE MONTH.`

segments.voice: Saga Dawa is the fourth month of the Tibetan calendar, usually falling around May or June. Dawa means month, or moon. Saga is the name of a star group, a lunar mansion the full moon sits near that month. So: the month of Saga. What makes it holy? In Tibetan tradition, the Buddha's birth, his awakening and his passing are all remembered in this month, with the big day on the full moon, called Saga Dawa Duchen, the great occasion. You may remember Vesak, where Theravada lands keep all three on one full moon. This is a Tibetan cousin of that same idea, with its own dates and customs: in Tibet, the birth is often marked on a different day, earlier in the month. Then comes the part people talk about most. Tibetan teachers say that during Saga Dawa, the effect of any action, good or harmful, is multiplied many times over. On the full moon, some say, by a hundred thousand. Nobody is keeping a ledger. The point is attention: a month when every small act counts for more, so you make them on purpose. So people do. They walk the pilgrim circuits, around the Jokhang, around Lhasa, and some walk all the way around Mount Kailash. Many families give up meat for the month. Some buy animals destined for slaughter and set them free. And they give, especially to anyone with a bowl out on the pilgrim route, because giving is at the head of the list of good deeds. Notice what that does to a month. Most of the year, a kindness is small. In Saga Dawa, it's treated as if it were large. And that's not a bad way to see one.
screen: `DAWA, MONTH. SAGA, A STAR.` · `BIRTH, AWAKENING, PASSING.` · `GOOD DEEDS MULTIPLIED.` · `CIRCLES, FREED ANIMALS, GIFTS.` · then, large: `THE HOLY MONTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give generously this month. Sit, and settle into the breath. Now let three people or causes come to mind, one at a time. Someone near you who could use something. Someone you pass every day and never really see. A cause you've meant to help and haven't. Hold each one for a few breaths. Ask quietly: what could I give? Time, money, food, attention, a letter. Don't decide everything now. Just let one gift become clear enough to act on. The bell holds the time.
Saga Dawa. The fourth Tibetan month, holding the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing, when good deeds are said to multiply. Today's word.
Your line: the holy month. Today, give the one gift that became clear in the sit, and treat it as if it counted a hundred times over. Day six hundred ninety-five.

screen: `DAY 695 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YEAR TWO CLOSE: HIS OWN WORDS.`

pairs: a star group the full moon sits near

a mountain some pilgrims walk around

myth: Saga Dawa is a single day
it's a whole month; the full moon, Saga Dawa Duchen, is its high point.
Tibetan teachers say both good and harmful actions are multiplied
the multiplying cuts both ways, so people act with care.

fork.setup: it's Saga Dawa. you're walking the pilgrim circuit in Lhasa, and every few steps someone sits with a bowl out. what do most pilgrims do?
options: walk past; the walking is the merit.
give small amounts to many of them.
give once at the end, to a temple.
fork.reveal: many pilgrims carry stacks of small notes and give to bowl after bowl; in this month, generosity is the point of the walk.

trapdoor: what you thought: saga dawa is a Tibetan name for the Buddha's birthday.
what it means: it's a whole month, holding his birth, awakening and passing, when good deeds are said to multiply.
what a scholar hears: saga is the Tibetan name of the lunar mansion called Vishakha in Sanskrit, the root of Vesakha.

sources.ref: Tibetan observance of Saga Dawa and Saga Dawa Duchen

696.title: Year two close: his own words
696.hook: the truths, the path, the middle-length, the long, the short, the connected, the numbered
696.howItsDone: Many Buddhists study the discourses through chanting, reading groups and Dhamma talks, and in many monasteries and homes a favorite verse or sutta line is recited daily or kept close as a reminder.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Saga Dawa, and your line, the holy month. Did you give the gift that came clear in the sit? Today is the last day of year two. Day six hundred ninety-six.

Three hundred sixty-five days ago, year two opened with a promise: the Buddha's own words. Not stories about him. Not commentary. The discourses themselves, as the early collections keep them. That's a lot of reading. Some days it was a single line. Some days it was a long walk through a long sutta. If you've been here most of those days, you've heard more of the Pali discourses than many people ever do. So today we stand at the lookout again, and pick up one line from each stretch of the road.
screen: `A YEAR OF HIS OWN WORDS.` → `ONE LINE FROM EACH STRETCH.`

segments.voice: First, the four noble truths. From the first sermon at the Deer Park, the whole map: there is suffering; it has a cause, which is craving; it can end; and there's a way. Then the eightfold path, factor by factor, six days each. View, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration. The line to keep: the middle way, between chasing pleasure and punishing yourself. Then the Middle-Length Sayings, read in order. From there, the raft: a teaching is like a raft you build to cross a river. You don't carry it on your head once you're across. Then the Long Discourses. From the last of the long road, the Buddha's advice in his final days: be an island to yourselves, a refuge to yourselves, with the teaching as your island. Then the short books: the Sutta Nipata, the Udana, the Itivuttaka. From the Sutta Nipata, the discourse on loving-kindness: as a mother would protect her only child with her life, so keep a boundless heart toward every living being. Then the Connected and the Numbered Sayings. From the Book of Threes, near the end of that stretch: keep the pot upright, so what's poured in stays. And last, the festival year: full moons, ghosts fed, robes sewn in a day, and the passing between the sal trees, all things end. There's an old Pali word for all of this: buddhavacana, the word of the Buddha. Schools of Buddhism draw the edges of that word differently. Theravada keeps the Pali canon. Mahayana schools also treasure sutras that year four will open, each in its own terms. This year we stayed with the early discourses. Not the whole forest. A good handful.
screen: `THE TRUTHS AND THE PATH.` · `THE RAFT AND THE ISLAND.` · `THE MOTHER AND THE UPRIGHT POT.` · `BUDDHAVACANA, HIS WORD.` · then, large: `YOU'VE READ HIS WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with one line from each. Settle, and let the breath find its pace. Then, slowly, one line per few breaths. Suffering has a cause, and an end. The middle way. The raft is for crossing. Be an island to yourself. A boundless heart, like a mother's. Keep the pot upright. All things end. Let each one land, then let it go. If one line stays longer than the others, let it. That might be the line for year three. The bell holds the time.
Year two close. A year of the Buddha's own words: the truths, the path, the middle-length, the long, the short, the connected and the numbered. Today's word.
Your line: you've read his words. Today, write down the one line from this year that stayed, and put it where you'll see it tomorrow. Year three begins with a poet. Day six hundred ninety-six.

screen: `DAY 696 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A POET TELLS THE LIFE.`

pairs: a mother protecting her only child

all Buddhist schools draw the edges of the Buddha's word the same way

fork.setup: you've built a raft and crossed the river. it served you well. what does the Buddha say to do with it?
options: carry it with you, out of gratitude.
leave it at the shore and go on.
burn it so no one else can use it.
fork.reveal: in the Middle-Length Sayings, the raft is for crossing over, not for holding onto; you leave it and walk on.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit buddhavacana: the word of the Buddha, what the schools count as his teaching.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha's words are one book.
what it means: they're whole collections: middle-length, long, short, connected, numbered.
what a scholar hears: the Nikayas, preserved orally for centuries and, tradition says, first written down in Sri Lanka in the first century BCE.

sources.ref: Mahaparinibbana Sutta, Digha Nikaya 16, II.26 (be an island to yourselves)
Avakujja Sutta, Anguttara Nikaya 3.30 (the upright pot)
